articles.title: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrests due to foreign body airway obstruction: A CanROC registry, retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: Foreign body airway obstruction (FBAO) is a treatable cause of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), but North American data are limited. Exploratory retrospective cohort study of EMS-treated OHCAs using the Canadian Resuscitation Outcomes Consortium (CanROC) registry (2005-2023), classified as obviously FBAO-related or of no obvious cause (presumed cardiac). Logistic regression compared Utstein characteristics between etiologies and identified factors associated with prehospital return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) and survival to acute care discharge. Among 105,178 EMS-treated OHCAs, 1,106(1.1%) were obviously FBAO-related. Compared with cases of no obvious cause, obviously FBAO-related cases were older (median 73 vs 68 years, p<0.001), more often witnessed (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 6.98[5.36-9.25]), more often attended by trained bystanders (aOR 3.30[2.41-4.41]), and less often had a shockable rhythm (aOR 0.11[0.07-0.15]). Obviously FBAO-related cases more often achieved prehospital ROSC (62.7% vs 37.8%; OR 2.77[2.44-3.13]), but survival did not differ (10.6% vs 9.0%,p=0.094). Within the obviously FBAO-related cohort, ROSC was associated with witnessed arrest (aOR 1.66[1.13-2.43]) and shorter EMS response time (aOR 0.95 per minute[0.92-0.99]). Survival was associated with younger age (aOR 0.76 per decade[0.61-0.93]), initial shockable rhythm (aOR 4.76[1.55-13.30]), and shorter EMS response time (aOR 0.81 per minute[0.66-0.98]). Survival was 18.1% and 0.8% among obviously FBAO-related OHCAs with and without prehospital ROSC, respectively. Obviously FBAO-related OHCAs are uncommon but clinically distinct. ROSC is frequent, yet survival remains low and is associated with early prehospital factors, supporting choking prevention initiatives, bystander training, and rapid EMS response.

articles.title: Commercially available multimodal LLMs for EEG-based prognostication after cardiac arrest.
articles.abstract: Machine-learning and deep-learning approaches have been successfully applied to EEG-based prognostication in comatose patients after cardiac arrest (CA), but typically rely on task-specific signal processing, feature extraction, and model development. Here, we investigated whether two commercially available multimodal large language models (LLMs) could predict neurological outcome directly from EEG images. Thirty-three comatose patients on the first day after CA from a prospective cohort were included. For each patient, a single 10-second EEG segment displayed using a longitudinal bipolar montage was rendered as PNG image. ChatGPT 5.4. and Claude Opus 4.7 were instructed to estimate the probability for favorable outcome for each case based on the EEG and a generic information block describing conditions of recordings. Five different prompting strategies were used, including few-shot prompting where four exemplary EEGs (not from the 33 patients) were provided. Predictive performance was quantified using AUC and accuracy. Across prompting strategies, the AUC ranged from 0.86 to 0.99 for ChatGPT and from 0.74 to 1.00 for Claude. The highest accuracy achieved by both models was 93.9% using few-shot prompting. As reference, a previously published dedicated deep-learning model achieved 100% on the same cohort. In this exploratory study of a small cohort, multimodal LLMs showed variable but potentially promising discrimination for predicting favorable outcome from single EEG image in comatose patients after CA. Performance depended substantially on prompt design. These findings require confirmation in a larger cohort.

articles.title: Community First Responder Activation Reduces the Negative Impact of AED Distance on Bystander Defibrillation After Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest.
articles.abstract: Early defibrillation is critical for survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), yet bystander defibrillation remains uncommon despite the availability of automated external defibrillators (AEDs). We investigated whether HeartRunner community first responder activation increased the likelihood of bystander defibrillation and 30-day survival in relation to the distance to the nearest accessible AED. Linking data from the Danish Cardiac Arrest Registry, Danish AED Network, and HeartRunner application, we identified patients with OHCA eligible for HeartRunner activation during 2017-2021. Using street-network distances to the nearest accessible AED, we examined associations between HeartRunner activation, bystander defibrillation, and 30-day survival using multivariable logistic regression with interaction terms and targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE). Among 5,753 OHCAs (median age, 74 years; 64% male; 78% in private locations), HeartRunner activation (41%) was associated with higher bystander defibrillation across AED distances (p-interaction = 0.004), with no interaction for 30-day survival (p-interaction = 0.054). Predicted bystander defibrillation with versus without HeartRunner activation was 9.6% vs 5.5% at Q1 (389 m), 10.0% vs 4.3% at median (717 m), and 13.0% vs 4.8% at Q3 (1,183 m). TMLE estimated a 6.1-percentage-point higher probability of bystander defibrillation (95% CI, 4.5-7.8; p<0.001) and a modest 1.8-percentage-point increase in 30-day survival (95% CI, 0.1-3.6; p=0.038) with HeartRunner activation. HeartRunner activation attenuated the decline in bystander defibrillation with increasing AED distance following OHCA, without a corresponding distance interaction for 30-day survival. Overall, TMLE supported higher bystander defibrillation and suggested a modest increase in 30-day survival with HeartRunner activation.

articles.title: Motorcycle gas-tank associated pelvic trauma: A scoping review of reported injury patterns, management and outcomes.
articles.abstract: Motorcycle gas-tank contact has been implicated in pelvic ring injury, often as part of a broader polytrauma presentation. This scoping review mapped reported injury morphology, associated injuries, management and outcomes according to the strength of tank-contact evidence. This scoping review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA-ScR guidance. MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Scopus and Web of Science databases were searched from inception to 20 September 2026. English-language clinical and forensic reports linking gas-tank contact to individually extractable pelvic ring injuries were included. Aggregate studies provided separate contextual evidence. Four contact-evidence tiers were grouped into higher-certainty and lower-certainty or inferred contact. Findings were synthesised descriptively using assessable denominators. Twenty studies reported 27 patients: 10 with higher-certainty and 17 with lower-certainty evidence of gas tank contact. Posterior-ring involvement was documented in 92% (22/24) of assessable patients while combined anterior-posterior injury occurred in 75% (18/24) assessable patients. Urinary, genital or perineal/scrotal/groin injury was documented in all patients in each group. Definitive pelvic fixation was reported in 15 patients with status unreported in 9 patients. Three deaths were reported. Follow-up was reported in 52% (14/27) of patients; mean follow-up was 8.3 months. Published gas tank-associated cases show recurring combined anterior-posterior pelvic ring disruption with adjacent genital or perineal trauma. Although selective reporting and uncertain contact attribution prevent confirmation of a gas tank-specific mechanism, these findings highlight the extent of pelvic ring involvement and associated soft-tissue injury. These findings provide an anatomical basis for future studies linking injury morphology with independently documented road traffic collision mechanisms.

articles.title: Pooled Prevalence of Infectious Diseases Among First Responders in the Prehospital Setting: A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis by Occupation.
articles.abstract: First responders often work in unpredictable, uncontrolled environments, where exposure to infected patients and contaminated environments heighten the risk of communicable disease transmission. Their higher infection prevalence compared with the general population has driven the implementation of personal protective equipment, vaccination requirements, safety protocols, and infection prevention education. The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to estimate the pooled prevalence of infections among first responders in the prehospital workers including paramedics, emergency medical technicians, patient transport staff, firefighters, police, and police officers. Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, and PUBMED/Medline were systematically searched. Pooled prevalence estimates were calculated using random-effects models with restricted maximum likelihood estimation, with Freeman-Tukey double-arcsine transformation and back-transformation to the original prevalence scale. Heterogeneity was assessed using I2, τ2, and 95% prediction intervals. Meta-regression was used to examine potential sources of between-study heterogeneity, and small-study effects and potential publication bias were assessed using funnel plots and Egger's regression test. Risk of bias was investigated using the AXIS tool. Following the initial search, 34,874 articles were identified, of which 88 were full-text screened. Of these, 22 studies representing 19,188 first responders were included in this systematic review. The pooled prevalences of hepatitis B and C were 6.2% (95% CI 4.5%-8.2%) and 1.8% (95% CI 0.9%-2.9%), respectively. Around 4% (95% CI 2.6%-5.9%) of the first responders had MRSA colonization. Current or past infection with COVID-19 among non-vaccinated first responders was 13.6% (95% CI 4.8%-25.9%), which reduced to 7.3% (95% CI 3.6%-12%) after exclusion of studies with high risk of bias. Of the known study characteristics, geographic region significantly contributed to heterogeneity, explaining 36.7% of between-study variance, p = 0.039. Infectious disease prevalence varied across pathogens, occupations, and geographical settings among first responders. These findings should be interpreted in light of substantial heterogeneity and limitations in the available evidence but may help inform infection prevention, occupational health policy, vaccination strategies, and future research in first responder services.

articles.title: Microbiota-gut-brain axis dysregulation in irritable bowel syndrome: mechanisms, clinical evidence, and therapeutic implications. a narrative review.
articles.abstract: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a heterogeneous disorder of gut-brain interaction in which altered visceral sensitivity, motility, immune activity, epithelial permeability, and microbial metabolism may interact. Microbiota-related associations are frequently reported, but their direction and causal relevance remain uncertain. This narrative review critically examines clinical and mechanistic evidence concerning microbiota-gut-brain communication in IBS, including short-chain fatty acids, bile acids, gaseous metabolites, tryptophan metabolism, environmental exposures, and microbiota-directed interventions. The literature was selected for relevance and interpretability rather than through a systematic evidence-synthesis protocol. Across studies, microbiota-associated differences vary by phenotype, diet, geography, sampling site, and analytical method; no validated IBS-specific microbial signature has emerged. Bile acid metabolism, mucosal immune-neural interactions, and microbial metabolites provide plausible mechanistic links, although much evidence remains associative. Low-FODMAP dietary treatment and rifaximin in appropriately selected patients have clinical trial support, whereas probiotic effects are formulation dependent and fecal microbiota transplantation remains investigational. Microbiome-based precision treatment requires longitudinal phenotyping, standardized sampling, functional multi-omics, and intervention studies demonstrating that microbial or metabolic changes mediate clinical benefit. Microbiome profiling is not yet established as a routine diagnostic test for IBS.

Transition-Phase Injuries and Wilderness EMS Operations During a Mountain Paragliding Festival: A Brief Report.
articles.abstract: IntroductionMountain paragliding festivals concentrate repeated takeoff, flight, and landing activity within terrain-dependent environments, potentially creating complex wilderness emergency medical services (EMS) demands. This brief report characterized festival-associated injury events, flight-phase distribution, environmental conditions, and EMS response requirements during a 2-day international mountain paragliding festival at Mount Babadağ, Turkey.MethodsWe retrospectively reviewed deidentified operational, prehospital, transport, and referral records for all festival-associated paragliding injury events. Variables included patient demographics, flight phase at injury, injury pattern, transport modality, prehospital acuity, and documented EMS resource utilization. Event-period meteorological conditions were summarized using hourly environmental data for the Mount Babadağ coordinate region.ResultsDuring the study period, 4716 paragliding flights and 13 injury events were recorded. The mean patient age was 41.5 ± 6.9 years. Ten injuries (76.9%) occurred during landing, 1 (7.7%) during takeoff, and 2 (15.4%) during sustained flight. Lower-extremity trauma predominated. Three patients were managed onsite, 8 were transported directly by ground ambulance, and 1 underwent maritime-to-ground ambulance transfer. One deceased pilot required helicopter-assisted postmortem recovery. Regional meteorological data showed mild temperatures and relatively low wind speeds.ConclusionsInjuries clustered around terrain-transition phases, especially landing. Mountain paragliding festivals require terrain-aware EMS planning, distributed response capability, and coordinated rescue and recovery resources.

articles.title: Seeing Beyond the Bowel: A Sentinel Loop as a Sonographic Clue to Pancreatobiliary Obstruction.
articles.abstract: The sentinel loop is a localized area of dilated bowel indicating localized abdominal inflammation, traditionally identified on plain films and computed tomography. Despite its diagnostic importance, sentinel loops have not been extensively characterized using point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) in pediatric populations. We report a case of a 3-year-old girl who presented with persistent abdominal pain, initially attributed to constipation. POCUS identified a sentinel loop associated with a choledochal cyst complicated by pancreatobiliary obstruction, an uncommon underlying pathology. Sonographic recognition of the sentinel loop redirected the diagnostic evaluation toward adjacent pathology in this case, illustrating its potential value as a contextual POCUS finding while underscoring the need for cautious interpretation given its nonspecificity and uncertain diagnostic performance.

Comparative validation of five early trauma scores for 24-hour in-hospital mortality in traumatic brain injury.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: Early risk stratification after traumatic brain injury (TBI) is crucial to guide monitoring, escalation of care, and interfacility transfer within the first hours. Bedside scores, including the "Revised Trauma Score (RTS)," "Glasgow Coma Scale, Age, and Systolic Blood Pressure score (GAP)," "modified Rapid Emergency Medicine Score (mREMS)," "Mechanism, Glasgow Coma Scale, Age, and Arterial Pressure score (MGAP)," and "Modified Early Warning Score (MEWS)," are simple and widely available. Prior studies often use mixed trauma cohorts, later endpoints, and provide limited evaluation of calibration or threshold-level clinical utility. TBI-specific head-to-head evidence is therefore needed. The five scores summarize different clinical domains. RTS incorporates the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS), systolic blood pressure (SBP), and respiratory rate; GAP incorporates GCS, age, and SBP; mREMS incorporates age, heart rate, respiratory rate, SBP, peripheral oxygen saturation, and GCS; MGAP incorporates injury mechanism, GCS, age, and arterial pressure; and MEWS incorporates routinely measured physiologic and neurologic variables, including blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, temperature, and level of consciousness. Diastolic blood pressure is not a component of any of the five scores evaluated in this study. The component structure and clinical domains of each score are summarized in Supplementary Table S1. This study analyzed consecutive traumatic brain injury admissions in 2024 at a tertiary medical center in Nantong, China (n = 2,287; 24-hour mortality 7.3%). The five bedside scores were recalibrated with a single logistic equation. Performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), the area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC), the Brier score, and calibration intercept and slope, while clinical utility was evaluated as net benefit per 100 patients at 10% and 20% thresholds. All estimates were reported with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) from 1,000 bootstrap resamples, and precision-recall curves were referenced to the cohort prevalence. RTS and GAP showed the strongest discrimination, with mREMS close. RTS 0.874 (95% CI 0.841-0.903), GAP 0.863 (0.831-0.898), mREMS 0.856 (0.826-0.883); MGAP and MEWS were lower (0.632, 0.606). AUPRCs were 0.465 (0.381-0.531) for RTS, 0.382 (0.308-0.453) for GAP, and 0.370 (0.280-0.424) for mREMS (MGAP 0.154 (0.112-0.199); MEWS 0.129 (0.098-0.159)). Brier scores were 0.050, 0.053, and 0.055 for RTS, GAP, and mREMS, respectively. After simple logistic recalibration, calibration intercepts were near 0 and slopes near 1, with observed-vs-predicted curves close to the 45° line across deciles. At 10% and 20% thresholds, RTS and GAP achieved the highest net benefit and more favorable trade-offs per 100 patients; mREMS was intermediate. RTS and GAP showed the best balance of discrimination, calibration, and net benefit at 10% and 20% thresholds; mREMS was comparable after simple recalibration. These findings support prioritizing RTS and GAP for early TBI risk stratification.

articles.title: [When a "minor" injury isn't so minor after all].
Needlefish Impalement Through the External Auditory Canal: CT Mapping of a High-Risk Penetrating Trajectory.
articles.abstract: Needlefish injuries are uncommon but potentially severe encounters in marine and coastal environments. The fish's elongated, toothed beak can produce a deep penetrating wound with little external evidence of its trajectory, creating an immediate challenge for field stabilization and transport. We describe a 47-year-old fisherman who sustained needlefish impalement through the left external auditory canal. Before referral, the fish body was cut away, while the head and beak were left in situ. Noncontrast computed tomography demonstrated a 7.73 cm calcified beak extending inferomedially through the parotid region to the prevertebral space at C1, with a penetration depth of approximately 5.6 cm and a small cortical defect in the left anterior arch of C1. No intracranial or spinal canal extension, large hematoma, or aerodigestive tract injury was identified. The beak passed close to the carotid vessels, although vascular injury could not be definitively excluded without angiographic imaging. Controlled surgical removal was completed without major vascular or neurologic complication. Complete removal was confirmed. At 1 month, the patient remained clinically well, and magnetic resonance imaging with angiography showed no delayed neurovascular complication. This case supports a practical sequence for marine impalement: stabilize the patient and embedded object, avoid field extraction, shorten only the external portion when necessary for safe transport without disturbing the penetrating segment, and transfer promptly to a center capable of cross-sectional imaging and controlled removal. Computed tomography defines the trajectory, while computed tomography angiography should be considered when major vessels may be involved.
