articles.title: Contextualized vs usual cardiopulmonary resuscitation skill stations: a simulation-based, randomized trial.
articles.abstract: We aimed to investigate whether training on a contextualized skill station combined with in-bed cardiopulmonary resuscitation instructions improves the number of excellent chest compressions in a simulated in-hospital cardiac arrest scenario compared to a standard table-based skill station. This randomized, multicenter trial included nurses and nurse assistants from two Danish emergency departments. Participants were trained in chest compressions on a contextualized skill station with the manikin on a bed (intervention) or on a skill station table (control). Participants completed two one-minute sessions with audiovisual feedback, repeated after 2-4 weeks. Skills were assessed in a 2-min in-hospital cardiac arrest scenario 4-8 weeks after the first training session. The primary outcome was the number of excellent chest compressions defined as guideline-compliant depth and rate. We included 65 participants. The intervention group training on the contextualized skill station performed more excellent compressions with a median (quartile 1; quartile 3) of 70 (27; 140) vs 23 (2; 93) (p = 0.01) compared to the control group. In addition, the intervention group performed more compressions with guideline-compliant depth (118 (53; 155) vs 78 (16; 127), p = 0.02), and more compressions with guideline-compliant rate (134 (86; 152) vs 58 (22; 134), p = 0.01) compared to the control group. More participants in the intervention group initiated compressions by jumping onto the bed (85%) compared to the control group (43%), p = 0.002. There was no significant difference in time to first compression. Training on a contextualized skill station with a manikin on a bed significantly increased the number of excellent chest compressions compared to skill station training with the manikin on a table. These findings highlight the importance of integrating clinical factors such as bed adjustments when implementing skill stations for CPR training in emergency departments to facilitate the transfer of skills.

articles.title: Terminology Without Consensus: A Thematic Analysis of Nomenclature Choice and Program Structure Among Expanded EMS Programs in a Single State.
articles.abstract: Expanded emergency medical services (E-EMS) programs, such as mobile integrated health care (MIH) and community paramedicine (CP), are increasingly common in the United States (U.S.). Although an international consensus definition exists specifically for CP, the terminology used by active U.S. E-EMS programs is poorly described, yet has important implications for program visibility, stakeholder engagement, evaluation, and policy. We sought to characterize how E-EMS programs in a single state describe themselves and factors associated with their chosen terminology. We conducted a qualitative thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews with E-EMS programs in Ohio. We used "E-EMS" as a historically established, neutral umbrella term to avoid prespecifying MIH, CP, or MIH-CP terminology during program identification. We identified E-EMS programs through voluntary reports to Ohio EMS, the Emergency Triage, Treat, and Transport (ET3) roster, publicly reported E-EMS programs on national dashboards, and snowball sampling. An interviewee from each E-EMS program participated in a recorded semi-structured interview focused on E-EMS program terminology, goals, services, and partnerships. Interview transcripts were reviewed by two coders, with discrepancies discussed with and adjudicated by a third reviewer. We used an inductive approach to develop the codebook, followed by thematic analysis to identify themes and subthemes. We identified 58 E-EMS programs meeting inclusion criteria; 23 participated and were included in the analysis. Participants described inconsistent use and varying interpretation of common terms such as MIH, CP, or MIH-CP; one in four used alternative terminology (e.g., neighborhood paramedic, EMS outreach). Participants attributed their terminology choices to the variability in MIH definitions and to limited understanding of MIH or CP among patients or external stakeholders. Despite variation in program terminology, program goals were consistently focused on filling unmet community needs, and program services were uniformly described as adaptable and reliant upon partnerships outside of EMS. The terminology used to describe E-EMS programs in a single state varied considerably. Despite this, E-EMS program goals and services were consistent, suggesting early convergence upon the core mission of E-EMS programs. Participants perceived inconsistent or unfamiliar terminology as a barrier to patient awareness, referral generation, and stakeholder engagement.

articles.title: More Than a Tobacco Problem: Cigarette Smoking as a Marker of Poorer Cardiovascular Health Among Emergency Medical Services Clinicians.
articles.abstract: Emergency medical services (EMS) work demands physical capacity, sustained alertness, and performance under stress, making cardiovascular health a workforce concern, not only a personal one. Cigarette smoking persists in portions of the EMS workforce, but whether it signals cardiovascular risk beyond tobacco exposure itself is unknown. We examined whether cigarette smoking was associated with poorer cardiovascular health across the non-tobacco domains of the American Heart Association's Life's Essential 8 (LE8) framework among nationally certified EMS clinicians. We conducted an observational study and cross-sectional secondary analysis of a voluntary survey offered to nationally certified emergency medical technicians (EMTs), advanced EMTs, and paramedics upon completion of recertification (October 2023-April 2024). To isolate associations beyond tobacco exposure, the primary outcome was a modified composite score (mLE7) averaging the seven non-nicotine LE8 domains (0-100 scale). Ideal cardiovascular health was defined as mLE7 ≥ 80. Multivariable linear and logistic regression models adjusted for demographic, educational, occupational, and organizational characteristics. Among 36,436 survey respondents, 7,703 had complete data for smoking status and all seven non-nicotine domains. Of these, 48.8% had never smoked, 45.2% formerly smoked, and 6.0% currently smoked. Mean mLE7 scores were 59.2 among never smokers, 56.9 among former smokers, and 51.5 among current smokers. Compared with never smokers, current smokers had lower adjusted mLE7 scores (β, -6.02; 95% CI, -7.63 to -4.41) and lower odds of ideal cardiovascular health (aOR, 0.37; 95% CI, 0.23 to 0.61). Former smokers had intermediate results (β, -1.62; 95% CI, -2.37 to -0.87; aOR, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.62 to 0.86). Current smoking was associated with poorer scores across diet, physical activity, sleep, blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood glucose domains (p < 0.05). Clinicians at private and hospital-based agencies had lower adjusted mLE7 scores than those at fire-based agencies. Among EMS clinicians, current cigarette smoking was associated with poorer cardiovascular health across nearly every non-tobacco domain, suggesting that smoking may serve as a readily identifiable marker of broader cardiovascular risk in this workforce. Agencies may consider pairing cessation support with broader cardiovascular health initiatives for clinicians who smoke. Sensitivity analyses addressing missing data yielded consistent results.

articles.title: Frequency of On-Scene Goal-Directed Field Interventions for Pediatric Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest in a Regional System of Care.
articles.abstract: Early on-scene resuscitation improves outcomes from pediatric non-traumatic out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA); however, for pediatric patients, the early evacuation strategy remains commonplace. We sought to determine the frequency of goal-directed interventions initiated by paramedics prior to transport for pediatric patients with OHCA in a regional emergency medical services (EMS) system. In this retrospective observational study and cross-sectional analysis, we analyzed the Cardiac Arrest Registry to Enhance Survival (CARES) and linked electronic patient care reports (ePCR) data for patients aged <15 years treated by EMS for nontraumatic OHCA in Los Angeles (LA) County from January 2021 to December 2022. The primary outcome was the frequency of goal-directed therapies administered on scene prior to transport, which we defined as defibrillation for shockable rhythms and administration of epinephrine and fluid resuscitation for non-shockable rhythms. We also tabulated descriptive statistics regarding arrest characteristics, scene times, frequency of other prehospital treatments, and patient outcomes. Among 176 eligible pediatric OHCA cases analyzed in CARES, 112 (64%) were male, the median age was 10 months (IQR 3-51), and 162 (92%) had an initial non-shockable rhythm. Of these, 156 patients were successfully linked to electronic patient care report (ePCR) records for analyses of prehospital interventions. Among 143 patients with non-shockable rhythms, EMS administered epinephrine before transport in 58 (41%) and fluids in 12 (8%). Among 13 patients with shockable rhythms, EMS delivered defibrillation before transport in 11 (85%). Bag-valve-mask (BVM) use was documented in 80 (51%) patients, although its timing relative to scene departure could not be determined. Median on-scene time was 10 minutes (IQR 5-18). Ten patients (6%) survived to hospital discharge, including 6 (3%) with a favorable neurologic outcome. In this regional EMS system, fewer than half of patients with non-shockable rhythms received a dose of epinephrine and fewer than one in ten received intravenous fluids prior to transport, whereas most patients with shockable rhythms were defibrillated on scene. Further work is needed to identify barriers to timely delivery of on-scene resuscitative interventions.

articles.title: Transcutaneous Pacing in the Prehospital Setting: A Retrospective Cohort Study of Electrical Capture.
articles.abstract: Transcutaneous pacing (TCP) treats hemodynamically unstable bradycardia refractory to pharmacologic management. Effective TCP requires electrical and mechanical capture to augment perfusion. Little is known about prehospital TCP and capture incidence. We conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients treated with prehospital TCP by an emergency medical services agency between 2017 and 2024. Continuous electrocardiogram recordings from cardiac monitors were reviewed. Electrical capture was the primary outcome, defined as a widened QRS with a distinct T wave following a TCP spike. Secondary measures included capture duration, clinician-verbalized pulse during pacing, plethysmograph waveform alignment, and changes in systolic blood pressure (SBP), pulse oximetry, and end-tidal carbon dioxide. Fifty-six patients received attempted TCP. Median age was 70 years (interquartile range [IQR] 58-85), and 34% were female. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) was administered in 59% of patients. Electrical capture was achieved in 18 patients (32%). Among patients who achieved electrical capture, complete capture occurred a mean of 27% (standard deviation 30%) of attempted pacing duration. The median SBP change was +22 (IQR: -2-82) mmHg in patients with electrical capture and 0 (IQR: -29-7) mmHg in those with only rare-to-absent capture (p = 0.031). During TCP, clinicians verbalized a palpable pulse 26 times across 19 patients. Only 4 instances (15%) coincided with electrical capture. Electrical capture during prehospital TCP occurred in a minority of patients and was often intermittent. Prehospital identification of mechanical capture using routine clinical indicators was difficult and unreliable. Future work should standardize capture definitions and physiologic measurements to determine when TCP produces clinically meaningful perfusion.

articles.title: An evaluation of the variability in the number of high-level trauma centers per million people in major metropolitan areas in the United States.
articles.abstract: The number of High-Level Trauma Centers (HLTCs) (Level I or II) per million people in major metropolitan areas is variable. The purpose of this study was to describe that variability and to determine if it was correlated with certain metropolitan area characteristics. A cross-sectional study of metropolitan areas with populations ≥ 2 million was performed using United States census data. The number of HLTCs per million people was calculated. The correlation between the number of HLTCs per million and the following variables was evaluated for: population density, race, land area, median household income, employment rate, uninsured rate, poverty rate, and public health insurance coverage rate. The association between State Certificate of Need (CON) laws for new trauma center development and HLTC per million, proportion of for-profit hospitals, and proportion of teaching hospitals was also evaluated. There were 35 metropolitan areas identified with a population of 2000,000 or more. The median number of HLTCs per million people was 1.51 (IQR 1.06-1.79) and ranged from 0.43 in Cincinnati to 3.93 in Chicago. The median ratio of level 1 to level 2 trauma centers located in each metropolitan area was 1.0 (IQR 0.5-1.7) and ranged from 0.25 to 5.0. Areas in states with a CON (n = 22), compared to those without a CON (n = 13), had a higher median percentile of teaching hospitals (100% vs. 76.9%, p = 0.01) and no observed difference in the median number of HLTCs per million (1.4 vs. 1.6, p = 0.5) or median percentile of for-profit HLTCs (0.0% vs. 10.0%, p = 0.65). The number of HLTCs per million was found to be negatively correlated with uninsured rates (R -0.33, p = 0.04) and was not correlated with population density, land area, race, median household income, employment rate, poverty rate, or the public health insurance coverage rate (p > 0.05). The number of HLTCs per million across major metropolitan areas varied widely. Metropolitan areas in states with a CON had a higher proportion of teaching hospitals. Cross-sectional study, Level IV.

articles.title: Presentation and treatment differences between upper extremity and lower extremity fracture-related infections.
articles.abstract: Fracture-related infection (FRI) presents a significant challenge with high rates of treatment failure and subsequent complication rates. To develop more effective and specific therapies for FRI, the purpose of this study is to analyze presentation, treatment, and outcomes of upper vs. lower extremity FRI, which were hypothesized to have distinct clinical profiles. Retrospective cohort at a Level 1 Trauma Center. Adult patients with operatively managed FRI from 2013 to 2020 with at least 6 months follow-up were included. Total operations, operations to clear infection, implant exchange, retention, and removal were compared between upper and lower extremity FRIs. One hundred forty-six patients were included. Forty-six had upper extremity FRI; 100 had lower extremity FRI. Mean follow-up was 2.7 years (SD 3.2). Lower extremity FRIs were significantly more likely to present with higher-grade soft tissue impairments (I) (p = 0.010). Implant failure at presentation was more common in upper extremity FRI compared to lower extremity FRI (41.3% vs. 15.0%, p = 0.001). Upper extremity FRI were more likely to be infected with C. acnes (17% vs. 0%, p < 0.001). Patients with upper extremity FRI had a lower median number of reoperations until FRI resolution (2 (1-3) vs. 3 (2-4), p = 0.006). Debridement, antibiotics, and implant retention, removal, and exchange were performed similarly in upper vs. lower extremity FRI. Causative bacteria, presentation characteristics and operative interventions required were different between upper and lower extremity FRIs. Upper and lower extremity FRIs exhibit distinct clinical profiles and prospective studies may be useful to compare extremity-specific treatment protocols. III.

articles.title: Traumaplasty for acetabular fractures: Factors associated with additional fracture fixation.
articles.abstract: Acute hip arthroplasty with additional fracture fixation, termed fix and replace (FAR), is an established option for selected acetabular fractures. The factors associated with adding fixation remain incompletely defined. We examined treatment selection in a mixed adult acetabular fracture cohort. This retrospective single-centre study included 29 adults undergoing hip arthroplasty for acetabular fractures, including periprosthetic or peri-implant injuries. Sixteen received FAR and 13 received arthroplasty without separate fracture fixation, termed fracture joint replacement (FJR). Preoperative computed tomography was used to measure fracture displacement. An exploratory logistic regression included maximum fracture displacement and Paprosky grade, with 26 complete cases. A sensitivity model additionally included articular displacement. Mean age was 72.8 ± 13.3 years (range 36-94); 20 patients were male and 10 had periprosthetic or peri-implant fractures. Mean maximum fracture displacement was 19.95 ± 10.00 mm in FAR and 6.66 ± 5.84 mm in FJR. In the two-predictor model, greater displacement was associated with FAR (odds ratio [OR] 1.22 per mm, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.03-1.46; p = 0.021). The Paprosky grade 3 estimate was imprecise (OR 4.41, 95% CI 0.47-41.85; p = 0.196). The model's 50% probability point was 9.7 mm when Paprosky grade was held at its cohort mean. Adding articular displacement attenuated the statistical evidence for the fracture-displacement association (p = 0.128). Greater fracture displacement was associated with additional fixation in an exploratory two-predictor model. The small, heterogeneous cohort and model sensitivity preclude a validated displacement threshold or a conclusion that fixation can safely be omitted. These findings require prospective validation.

articles.title: [Stress factors and coping strategies in the nursing and care of patients with a left ventricular assist device (LVAD) suffering from treatment-resistant heart failure-a qualitative study of nursing staff in German intensive care units].
articles.abstract: Critical care nurses play a vital role in the care of patients with a left ventricular assist device (LVAD) and must be able to cope with various challenges. The aim of this study was to gain insight into the experiences of critical care nurses in caring for patients with a LVAD, to identify potential stressors, and thereby to determine the need for support. As part of a qualitative research design, nine intensive care nurses from Germany were interviewed between April and June 2025 using semi-structured, guided interviews. Data analysis was conducted using content analysis structured according to Kuckartz. The greatest challenges for intensive care nurses were a lack of knowledge regarding the specific nursing requirements and the use of the LVAD, as well as structural and personnel-related conditions. While coping strategies are already in place, the majority of nurses would like to expand their knowledge. By identifying various stressors, specific support services can be expanded or established for everyday clinical practice. Potential measures include building and regularly updating foundational knowledge through structured training programs, as well as ensuring that counseling services are readily available. In addition, specialized communication training and standardized work procedures are recommended.

articles.title: What's Blood Got to Do with It? Identifying MPDS® Dispatch Codes Most Commonly Associated with Prehospital Blood Administration.
articles.abstract: This study aimed to identify Medical Priority Dispatch System (MPDS®) codes most frequently associated with prehospital blood utilization. We examined Delaware's prehospital blood database to determine dispatch codes where low titer group O positive whole blood (LTOWB) was administered. We calculated the number of blood units under each dispatch code within the study period (May 2023- February 2026). Using this data, we identified the MPDS® codes associated with the highest number of blood units, including the top five codes overall, top medical codes, and as well as blood utilization rates for penetrating versus blunt traumas. The most frequent blood utilization came from the following dispatch codes: 29D02 (traffic collision, high mechanism) 32 patients, 27D04G (penetrating trauma with central wounds) 32 patients, 29D02M (auto versus pedestrian) 28 patients, 29D05 (traffic collision with entrapment) 24 patients, and 29D02L (auto versus bicycle/motorcycle) 20 patients. These five dispatch codes accounted for 29% of all prehospital LTOWB utilized within the 33-month study period. Analyzing blood utilization for non-traumatic dispatch codes revealed: 21D04/21D04M (dangerous hemorrhage, medical) 18 patients, 21D03/21D03M (hemorrhage, not alert, medical) 13 patients, 9E01/M9E01/M9E02 (cardiac or respiratory arrest/death, not breathing) 13 patients, and 21D05/21D05M (hemorrhage, abnormal breathing, medical) 7 patients. These four dispatch codes accounted for 11% (51 patients) of LTOWB utilization. When performing odds ratio analysis to determine odds of blood administration, we found 27D04G, 29D02M, and 29D02L to be statistically significant with 95% confidence intervals of [0.35- 0.87], [2.42- 5.72], [1.47- 3.91], and odds ratios of 0.55, 3.72, and 2.40, respectively. Additionally, our analysis demonstrated that patients with MPDS® coding for penetrating trauma with a delta level priority (27D) have higher likelihood of prehospital blood administration than delta priority high mechanism traffic incidents (29D). This comparison showed an OR of 10.40 that blood would be given to the penetrating trauma patient with a 95% confidence interval of [7.93- 13.66]. Specific MPDS® codes are strongly associated with prehospital blood utilization. Identifying these patterns offers a unique opportunity for emergency medical services systems to implement automatic blood dispatch protocols based on dispatch code.

articles.title: Prolonged Onboard Storage of Red Blood Cells in Ground Ambulances for Prehospital Transfusion: A Real-World Study.
articles.abstract: Permanent onboard storage of red blood cells (RBC) units could facilitate timely prehospital transfusion but may expose blood products to cumulative transport-related mechanical stress. We evaluated the quality of RBC units stored continuously in operational ground ambulances under real-world emergency medical service conditions. In this randomized controlled experimental study of RBC units, leukoreduced RBC units were randomly assigned to continuous onboard ambulance storage from day 7 to day 42 (n = 12) or standard blood bank storage at 2-6 °C for 42 days (n = 14). Samples were analyzed on days 7, 28, and 42. The primary outcome was hemolysis. Secondary outcomes included plasma biochemistry and storage-induced microerythrocytes (SMEs), an emerging morphological marker associated with post-transfusion RBC recovery. Temporal trajectories of SME levels were assessed using repeated-measures multivariate analysis of variance and fixed-effects panel models. All RBC units remained below the European regulatory hemolysis threshold of 0.8% at day 42. Hemolysis was higher in ambulance-stored units at day 28 (Hodges-Lehmann difference, +0.043 percentage points; 95% confidence interval (CI), 0.010-0.076; p = 0.015) and day 42 (+0.096 percentage points; 95% CI, 0.029-0.176; p = 0.008). The SME levels increased in both groups, with a significant time-by-group interaction (p = 0.034) indicating different temporal trajectories. Additional SME accumulation in ambulance-stored units occurred predominantly between days 28 and 42. At day 42, the mean between-group SME difference was +9.04 percentage points (95% CI, -0.66 to 18.73; p = 0.066). The available sample was insufficient to exclude moderate or larger between-group differences. Biochemical changes were broadly similar between groups. Continuous onboard RBC storage in operational ground ambulances maintained all units within regulatory hemolysis limits through day 42. However, higher hemolysis and late divergence in SME accumulation suggest that prolonged ambulance exposure may influence RBC storage quality. These findings provide preliminary support for the feasibility of continuous onboard RBC storage, particularly earlier in the storage period, but do not establish equivalence with conventional blood bank storage.

articles.title: Early arthroplasty versus conversion arthroplasty after failed PFNA in elderly patients with unstable intertrochanteric fractures: a multicenter matched cohort study.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: In our study, the clinical and functional outcomes of early arthroplasty versus late conversion arthroplasty approaches were compared in individuals over 75 years of age who underwent PFNA for complex intertrochanteric fractures but whose treatment failed. This multicenter, retrospective cohort study analyzed data from 136 patients treated between January 2023 and March 2025. The cohort consisted of 62 patients who underwent conversion arthroplasty after failed PFNA fixation and 74 patients who received primary early arthroplasty. Demographic characteristics, surgical parameters, complications, and functional and rehabilitation outcomes were compared between groups. Early arthroplasty was associated with significantly better six-month functional outcomes, including higher Parker mobility and Merle d'Aubigné scores. The early arthroplasty group also demonstrated shorter times to effective weight-bearing and recovery of walking distance. Perioperative transfusion requirements and systemic complication rates were higher in the PFNA conversion group. However, the time to recovery of unassisted gait did not differ significantly between groups. Conclusion In elderly patients over 75 years of age with unstable intertrochanteric fractures, early arthroplasty was associated with better short-term functional outcomes, earlier effective weight-bearing and recovery of walking distance, and fewer systemic complications than conversion arthroplasty following failed PFNA. However, these findings should be interpreted in the context of the retrospective design and the functional deterioration that occurred between initial PFNA and subsequent conversion surgery. Primary arthroplasty may be a reasonable option in carefully selected patients with fracture patterns, poor bone quality, or clinical characteristics associated with a high risk of fixation failure.

articles.title: Prehospital Trauma Compendium: Prehospital Management of Pediatric Traumatic Out-of-Hospital Circulatory Arrest - A Joint Position Statement and Resource Document of NAEMSP, ACS-COT, ACEP, and AAP.
articles.abstract: In 2014 the National Association of EMS Physicians (NAEMSP), American College of Surgeons Committee on Trauma (ACS-COT), American College of Emergency Physicians (ACEP), and American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) published the first joint position statement discussing withholding and discontinuing resuscitation attempts for pediatric traumatic out-of-hospital circulatory arrest (TOHCA). Since then, the body of literature addressing pediatric TOHCA has evolved and evidence has grown that demonstrates the nearly uniformly poor prognosis of children who suffer circulatory arrest in the prehospital setting as a result of trauma. To support emergency medical services (EMS) clinicians in their approach to these high-acuity, low-frequency, and challenging cases, this project aimed to update guidance regarding decisions to withhold or discontinue resuscitation efforts for pediatric traumatic circulatory arrest. NAEMSP, ACEP, ACS-COT, and AAP recommend:EMS resuscitation of pediatric TOHCA should:Prioritize prompt identification of patients who may benefit from transport to definitive care at trauma centers when safe and appropriate. On-scene resuscitation should be balanced against the potential benefit of transfer to a proximate trauma center.Emphasize the identification of reversible causes of traumatic circulatory arrest and timely use of clinically indicated life-saving interventions (LSIs) within the EMS clinician's scope of practice. These include:External hemorrhage control with direct pressure, wound packing, and tourniquetsAirway management using the least-invasive airway interventions required to achieve and maintain airway patency, oxygenation, and adequate ventilation.Chest decompression if clinical concern for tension pneumothorax. Empiric bilateral decompression is not recommended in the absence of suspected thoracic trauma.External chest compressions and ventilations have a larger role in pediatric TOHCA resuscitation than in adult TOHCA resuscitation, with children frequently having TOHCA secondary to head injury, hypoxia and other non-hemorrhagic mechanisms. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) should be provided when the cause of circulatory arrest is unclear.Epinephrine is of lower priority than other LSIs.Consider point of care ultrasound (POCUS) to guide decisions to withhold or discontinue resuscitation efforts.Resuscitation attempts may be withheld in pediatric TOHCA patients with:Injuries that are incompatible with life (e.g., decapitation, hemi-corpectomy, incineration).Evidence of prolonged circulatory arrest (e.g., rigor mortis, dependent lividity, decomposition).Advanced care planning documents that indicate Do Not Resuscitate (DNR)/ Do Not Attempt Resuscitation (DNAR)/Allow Natural Death medical orders.Resuscitation attempts may be discontinued in pediatric TOHCA patients who:Have no return of spontaneous circulation after provision of at least 15 minutes of high-quality CPR in addition to performance of other lifesaving interventions directed at treating potentially reversible causes of pediatric TOHCA. Longer durations of CPR, up to 30 minutes, may be considered for patients with positive predictors of survival such as organized rhythm, witnessed arrest, bystander CPR, or with proximate access to a trauma center.Have known predictors of very low probability of survival such as penetrating trauma without proximate access to a trauma center, asystole, unwitnessed arrest, or lack of bystander CPR.Protocols guiding decisions to withhold or discontinue resuscitation of pediatric TOHCA benefit from oversight by EMS physicians in collaboration with pediatric experts and local or regional trauma system stakeholders. Implementation of such protocols for pediatric patients benefits from involvement of community stakeholders including family representatives, law enforcement, medical examiner, and child fatality review committees.Considerations for protocol implementation include local resource availability, EMS clinician and public safety, psychosocial support to surviving family members and emergency responders, and dignified handling of the deceased patient.Training needs for EMS clinicians include techniques to communicate with family members regarding the death of a child and understanding the clinician's own response to this low-frequency, high-emotion experience.

articles.title: Development of a Comprehensive Pediatric Burn Outcome Measure: The School-Aged Life Impact Recovery Evaluation Instrument.
articles.journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
articles.abstract: Assessing health-related quality of life in school-aged children remains challenging in pediatric burn care, underscoring the need for developmentally appropriate tools to monitor recovery. This study evaluated the psychometric properties of the School-Aged Life Impact Burn Recovery Evaluation (SA-LIBRE5-12) Profile, a parent-reported measure for burn survivors aged 5-12 years. Parents field-tested 195 items for the development of the SA-LIBRE5-12 Profile using frequency and ability response scales. Items were scored from 0 to 4, with higher scores indicating better functioning. Factor analysis was used to identify unidimensional domains. Item response theory analyses estimated item parameters and calibrated item banks. Computer Adaptive Test simulations generated scale scores, which were compared with full item bank scores based on score range, floor and ceiling effects, and marginal reliability. The sample included 416 parents of pediatric burn survivors. Children had a mean age of 8.5 ± 2.4 years, 54.3% were male, mean total body surface area burned was 8.7%, and mean time since injury was 4.5 years. An eight-factor structure emerged: Functional Impact of Burn Symptoms (17 items), Upper Extremity (15), Lower Extremity (11), Psychosocial (22), Resilience (6), Body Image (13), Peer Relations (10), and School (6). CATs were developed for all domains except Resilience, Peer Relations, and School due to limited item counts. Correlations between CAT and full-bank scores ranged from 0.94 to 0.99 (p<0.05), with marginal reliabilities between 0.61 and 0.87. The SA-LIBRE5-12 Profile is a psychometrically sound, multidimensional measure for assessing recovery-related outcomes in children aged 5-12 years following burn injury.

articles.title: Ultrasound-guided hydrostatic reduction of intussusception: a practical guide with a focus on low-resource settings.
articles.abstract: Ultrasound-guided hydrostatic reduction (UGHR) is a safe, effective, and reproducible technique for the management of pediatric intussusception. However, there remains a lack of standardized, practical guidance on the implementation and performance of UGHR. To present a practical, standardized framework for UGHR, emphasizing safe implementation across diverse clinical settings. This practical review outlines a step-by-step approach based on clinical experience and existing literature, including patient selection, pre-procedural preparation, equipment setup, procedural technique, criteria for success and failure, and troubleshooting strategies. The proposed framework is applicable across a wide range of healthcare environments and may be particularly advantageous in low-resource settings where access to fluoroscopic resources is limited.

articles.title: Pseudo-continuous arterial spin labeling (pCASL): a practical clinical guide to contrast-free cerebral perfusion imaging in stroke and steno-occlusive disease.
articles.abstract: The past decade has witnessed the emergence of multiple arterial spin labeling (ASL)-based imaging techniques, with growing evidence supporting their utility across diverse neurological diseases. ASL represents a paradigm shift in perfusion imaging as a noninvasive, contrast-free MRI technique that provides both cerebral perfusion quantification and detection of arterial stenosis or occlusion, offering diagnostic capabilities comparable to the established dynamic susceptibility contrast (DSC) technique while avoiding contrast-related risks. This review article provides a focused clinically oriented overview of Pseudo-continuous arterial spin labeling (pCASL) technique in stroke imaging, discusses the fundamental physical principles of arterial spin labeling, examines various acquisition and optimization strategies, and evaluates clinical applications with primary emphasis on acute ischemic stroke and steno-occlusive cerebrovascular disease, the predominant risk factor for recurrent stroke.

articles.title: Predicting mortality in pediatric cases with severe traumatic brain injury: is the Eppendorf-Cologne Scale more reliable than Glasgow Coma Scale?
authors: TraumaRegister DGU® of the German Trauma Society (Deutsche Gesellschaft für Unfallchirurgie; DGU)
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: Severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) in children is a major cause of morbidity and mortality, requiring reliable tools for early assessment and prognosis. While the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is the standard neurological evaluation tool, it has limitations in pediatric patients. The Eppendorf-Cologne Scale (ECS), originally developed for adults, emphasizes pupil size, reactivity, and motor response and may offer advantages in children. This multicenter cohort study analyzed TraumaRegister DGU® data from 5,851 pediatric patients (mean age 9.6 years). Documentation included prehospital and in-hospital assessments, injury characteristics, and outcomes. ECS and GCS scores were evaluated based on first recorded prehospital values. Predictive performance for mortality and severe TBI was assessed using AUROC analysis. Among the cohort, 2,582 patients (44.1%) had severe TBI and 476 (8.1%) died in hospital. GCS showed slightly higher accuracy for predicting severe TBI (AUROC 0.778, 95% CI 0.766-0.791) than ECS (AUROC 0.745, 95% CI 0.731-0.758). For mortality prediction, ECS performed marginally better (AUROC 0.943, 95% CI 0.929-0.957) than GCS (AUROC 0.910, 95% CI 0.896-0.924). Mortality rates were 90% in the worst ECS category and 55% in the worst GCS category. GCS showed higher discrimination for severe TBI, whereas ECS showed higher discrimination for in-hospital mortality among patients with severe TBI. ECS may provide complementary prognostic information, but its clinical utility and role alongside GCS require prospective evaluation.

articles.title: Blunt anatomical cardiac injury (BACI) - lessons from a single trauma center cohort.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: Patients with anatomical damage to the heart after blunt trauma are rarely seen in hospital settings due to their elevated prehospital mortality. The aim of this study is to review our center experience with this entity. After institutional research board approval, a local Trauma Databank search (Qatar National Trauma Registry) was performed from 2016 to 2025. Cases presented with blunt trauma and anatomical changes to pericardium or heart, detected in imaging or surgery, in patients above 13 years old were diagnosed as blunt anatomical cardiac injury - BACI and included. Amongst 17542 blunt trauma cases admitted to our Trauma Center during the study period, 15 patients (0.09% incidence) met the inclusion/exclusion criteria. All patients were males, with average age of 43 years (ranges 26-75), with ISS of 32 (ranges 10-75). The most common mechanism of injury was pedestrian struck (5cases -33%). Hypotension at trauma room assessment was common (8 cases - 53% of patients) and 8 patients (53%) required surgery. FAST, echocardiogram and computed tomography were used as diagnostic tools. The patients presented in 4 anatomical patterns: (a) intracardiac/valve damage; (b) pericardial effusion; (c) pericardial laceration and (d) cardiac rupture. Three patients (20%) died, all during emergent surgery and sustaining cardiac rupture. BACI is uncommonly seen at Emergency Departments and carries elevated early mortality in cases with cardiac rupture, requiring high index of suspicion for diagnosis. Different clinical presentations of BACI were observed and described in this series. Further studies with larger number of patients are needed to further clarify possible differences in severity, surgical requirement and mortality according to the BACI structural presentation.

articles.title: Projections of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease incidence and its driving factors in 195 countries and territories to 2050: a modeling study.
articles.abstract: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) remains a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality. This study aims to characterize historical trends in COPD burden from 1990 to 2021, project incidence through 2050 by age, sex, year, and location, and quantify the impact of key risk factors on future COPD incidence. We analyzed historical COPD burden across 204 countries and territories using Global Burden of Disease 2021 estimates from 1990 to 2021, including incidence, prevalence, mortality, and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs). Temporal trends were evaluated using Joinpoint regression and Age-Period-Cohort (APC) modeling. Future COPD incidence was projected to 2050 for 195 countries and territories with compatible age-, sex-, year-, and location-specific population forecasting data using a Bayesian Age-Period-Cohort (BAPC) model. Population attributable and impact fractions were calculated to estimate the benefits of reducing modifiable exposures. By 2050, global COPD incidence is projected to continue rising with annual new cases expected to reach 32.3 (95%UI 13.6-50.9) million, though the age-standardized rate may decline by 3.0%. Although sex disparities are narrowing, significant geographic inequalities will persist. China, India, and the United States are forecasted to remain the largest contributors, jointly accounting for nearly half of global incident cases. Eliminating smoking and ambient particulate matter pollution could prevent up to 33.0% and 30.1% of new cases, respectively. Despite modest declines in age-standardized incidence rates, the absolute number of new COPD cases is projected to nearly double by 2050. Marked disparities by age, sex, and geography highlight the need for targeted and equitable public health interventions. Strengthening tobacco control and air pollution mitigation policies could prevent millions of future cases and significantly reduce the global COPD burden.

articles.title: Pediatric Frostbite and Cold-Weather Injuries in the United States: A Multi-Database Retrospective Analysis.
articles.journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
articles.abstract: Pediatric cold-weather injuries (frostbite and hypothermia) are uncommon but can lead to substantial morbidity, including amputation and long-term functional loss. National data on incidence, management, and outcomes are limited, particularly for fatalities outside healthcare settings. We conducted a retrospective analysis using three complementary data sources: an institutional registry at an American Burn Association-verified burn center (2018-2026), the Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project National Readmission Database (NRD 2016-2021), and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Storm Events Database (NOAA 2016-2023). Our institutional cohort included 16 patients (ages 1-17 years; 68.8% >13 years); treatments included rapid rewarming (43.8%), perfusion imaging (56.3%), thrombolytic therapy (18.8%), and hyperbaric oxygen therapy (31.3%). Two patients required amputation; both presented with hemorrhagic blisters, had delayed care, and did not receive thrombolytics. No thrombolytic-related complications were observed. Nationally, 2,155 pediatric cold weather injuries occurred; a national estimated hospitalization rate of 1.62 per 100,000. 79 pediatric frostbite admissions were identified, including 15 admissions designated as severe injury. NOAA data captured 16 pediatric deaths and 49 injuries across 30 states. Pediatric cold-weather injuries result in morbidity and mortality across diverse U.S. regions. Early aggressive management may reduce amputation and broader adoption of standardized protocols and public health prevention strategies are needed. Limitations of public health data emphasize the need for integrating diverse data sources to better understand the full impact of cold-weather injuries in the U.S.

articles.title: Partner Consultation to Inform Comparative Effectiveness Research on Frostbite Treatment: A Multi-Method Community Engagement Study.
articles.journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
articles.abstract: Frostbite causes severe tissue injury frequently requiring amputation. Functional outcomes following frostbite injury are underreported, and no published literature describes a stakeholder-informed approach to frostbite research design incorporating patient, provider, or community perspectives. A multi-method stakeholder consultation was conducted to inform a Comparative Effectiveness Research (CER) grant proposal. The aim of this report is to share the community perspectives gathered during consultation, to support others designing frostbite research, and to demonstrate a replicable engagement process for rare, acute injury research. Sixteen participants were recruited through collaborative clinical sites, Healthcare for the Homeless, and the International Frostbite Resource Group. Eleven completed an online survey and eleven participated in virtual group meetings; persons with prior frostbite injury were offered optional 1:1 meetings. Survey data were analyzed descriptively; meeting transcripts were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. This report follows GRIPP2 and SRQR reporting guidelines. Reducing severe cases and amputations was the most endorsed outcome priority, though survivors identified cold sensitivity, fine motor function, grip strength, and return to activities as the outcomes with the greatest impact on daily life. Three qualitative themes emerged: barriers to care are multilayered and mutually reinforcing; patient-centered outcomes extend beyond amputation prevention; and important clinical questions and care needs remain unaddressed. This community partner consultation demonstrates that improving outcomes requires not only advances in treatment, but systems enabling timely access to care and addressing structural barriers for high-risk populations.

articles.title: Hypophosphatemia in Pediatric Diabetic Ketoacidosis: Incidence, Determinants, and Clinical Impact in a Tertiary Emergency and Intensive Care Cohort.
articles.abstract: Serum phosphate levels commonly decline during treatment of pediatric diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), but the determinants and clinical implications of hypophosphatemia remain incompletely defined. We aimed to determine its incidence, predictors, and clinical impact during pediatric DKA. In this retrospective study, 116 DKA episodes managed in a tertiary pediatric emergency department and intensive care unit between January 2022 and June 2025 were analyzed. Demographic characteristics, admission biochemical parameters, and clinical outcomes were recorded. Hypophosphatemia was defined according to age-specific reference ranges. Multivariable logistic regression identified independent predictors of hypophosphatemia, while length of hospital stay was assessed using multivariable linear regression of log-transformed values. Hypophosphatemia occurred in 72/116 episodes (62.1%). Compared with those without hypophosphatemia, affected patients had lower admission pH (7.03±0.13 vs. 7.12±0.17; P=0.002), bicarbonate (7.8±2.4 vs. 9.8±3.3 mEq/L; P<0.001), and potassium levels (4.43±0.96 vs. 4.81±0.66 mEq/L; P=0.024). Hyponatremia and hypokalemia were more frequent, whereas hyperkalemia was less common (all P<0.05). Lower admission pH (OR: 0.008, 95% CI: 0.000-0.219; P=0.004) and lower baseline phosphate concentration (OR: 0.67, 95% CI: 0.47-0.97; P=0.031) independently predicted hypophosphatemia. Although hospitalization was longer in the hypophosphatemia group (85.3±75.2 vs. 56.2±36.4 h; P=0.018), hypophosphatemia was not independently associated with length of stay. Higher admission pH independently predicted shorter hospitalization (β=-0.957, P=0.026). Baseline phosphate positively correlated with nadir phosphate during treatment (r=0.303, P<0.001). Hypophosphatemia is common during pediatric DKA and is closely associated with the severity of metabolic acidosis at presentation. However, it does not independently affect hospitalization duration, suggesting that it primarily reflects disease severity rather than independently determining short-term outcomes.

articles.title: Just the facts: emergency diagnosis and management of severe hyperkalemia.
For emergency department patients with alcohol withdrawal syndrome, a comorbid mood disorder is associated with increased system utilization representing illness burden.
articles.abstract: The impact of comorbid mood disorders on emergency department revisits and hospitalizations among patients presenting with alcohol withdrawal is not well understood. We compared ED revisits and hospitalizations among those patients with alcohol withdrawal and mood disorder to those without mood disorder. We included unique patients who presented to EDs in Vancouver, Canada, with a diagnosis of alcohol withdrawal. Structured chart reviews ascertained comorbidities and defined the presence of mood disorder based on documented diagnosis at or before the index visit. The primary and secondary outcomes were any ED visit or hospitalization in the subsequent year. We describe differences between patients using absolute difference and 95% confidence intervals [CI]. We identified 1010 unique patients; the median age was 46 (range 15-79), 73% were male, and 403 (40%) had a mood disorder. By 1 year, 78% of patients with mood disorders had at least one ED revisit, compared to 61% of patients without (difference 17% [11-22%]). Among patients with mood disorders, the median number of return visits was 3 [1-8] compared to 1 [0-5] for a patient with no mood disorder. By 1 year, 35% of patients with a mood disorder had ≥ 1 hospital admission versus 21% of patients without (difference 14% [8.5-20%]). Among patients with alcohol withdrawal, those with mood disorders had nearly double the number of ED visits and more frequently required hospital admission within 1 year. These findings underscore the need for targeted interventions for patients with alcohol withdrawal and mood disorders.

articles.title: A Mobile Application Improves Paramedic Performance in Simulated Trauma Care: A Crossover Randomized Controlled Trial.
articles.abstract: Clinical performance during prehospital trauma care varies among emergency medical services (EMS) clinicians, particularly during high-stress critical responses. We developed a mobile application providing real-time access to local treatment protocols, decision support tools, and instructional procedure videos to supplement standard practice. We evaluated whether use of the application improved paramedic performance during simulated trauma scenarios. We conducted a crossover randomized controlled trial between July 2025 and February 2026 comparing standard care alone with standard care plus the mobile application during two high-fidelity trauma simulations (one adult and one pediatric). Paramedics, working in pairs, were block randomized to one of four sequences, varying both the scenario order and the application use. Performance was assessed using predefined critical actions; completing all critical actions was required to successfully complete the scenario. A generalized linear mixed model with a binomial distribution and logit link function was used for each paramedic pair to estimate the adjusted odds ratio (OR) for successfully completing a scenario with or without the application. Of 112 paramedics, 98 (88%) participated, forming 49 pairs. One pair withdrew before study completion, leaving 48 pairs for analysis. For scenarios using the application, 17/48 (35.4%) successfully completed the scenario compared to 3/48 (6.3%) for scenarios not using the application, adjusted odds 8.28 (95% CI 2.21-31.09). Among scenarios using the application, 10/25 (40%) adult scenarios and 7/23 (30.4%) pediatric scenarios met successful completion criteria compared to 3/23 (13%) adult and 0/25 (0%) pediatric with standard practice alone. User experience survey results demonstrated that participating paramedics assessed the application as being practical to use and valuable for clinical care. Use of the mobile decision support application improves odds of performing high-quality clinical care in simulated trauma patient scenarios. Further studies are needed to evaluate performance and usability in a field environment.

articles.title: Five-Year Experience with Automated Head Up Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation for Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest.
articles.abstract: Automated head-up position cardiopulmonary resuscitation (AHUP-CPR), the combination of a head and thorax positioning device, active compression-decompression CPR, and an impedance threshold device, lowers intracranial pressure and increases cerebral blood flow and neurologically favorable survival in animal models versus conventional CPR (C-CPR). This prospective, observational, investigator-initiated registry study reports 5-year multi-center outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) from areas served by emergency medical services (EMS) agencies that implemented AHUP-CPR as their routine first-responder standard of care. Adults with non-traumatic OHCA were initially treated with immediate conventional (C-CPR) followed by rapid transition to AHUP-CPR. The primary study focus was on patients who survived to hospital discharge with favorable neurological function (HD-FN). Additional analyses included assessment of sustained return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), survival to hospital discharge (HD), outcomes based upon the presenting rhythm, and impact of covariates on HD-FN. Ten EMS agencies serving 1.5 million people across nine U.S. states contributed data to the AHUP-CPR Registry. A total of 3,709 OHCA patients met enrollment criteria. Across five years, (2020-2024), the average (± SD) interval from 9-1-1 call receipt-to-professional CPR was 9.62 ± 5.78 min. Incidence of ROSC, HD, and HD-FN were 29.5%, 13.1%, and 10.5%, respectively. The incidence of HD-FN for patients presenting with a shockable rhythm meeting Utstein criteria, pulseless electrical activity, or asystole were 33.9%, 11.8%, and 2.0%, respectively. Among 391 neurologically favorable survivors, 91% had a Cerebral Performance Category score of 1 (normal or near normal brain function) at HD. The average age of the survivors was 56.8 ± 16.3 years. Age, interval from 9-1-1 call to professional CPR, witnessed status, and initial rhythm were the most significant predictors of HD-FN using multivariable Poisson regression. In this 5-year observational registry study, use of AHUP-CPR for the treatment of OHCA was associated with survival to HD of 13.1% and HD-FN of 10.5% in the overall cohort, which comprised patients presenting in shockable rhythms, PEA, and asystole. Drawn from 3,709 OHCA patients treated across diverse EMS systems, these findings provide the largest clinical practice-based characterization to date of the outcomes associated with early transition to AHUP-CPR.

articles.title: Prehospital Resource Utilization After Video-Assisted Versus Telephone-Only Emergency Calls: A Post Hoc Analysis of the CAM-VISION Cluster Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.abstract: To examine whether video assistance during emergency calls reduced actual prehospital resource utilization across the complete response pathway compared with telephone-only calls. This post hoc analysis included 18,745 calls from the cluster-randomized CAM-VISION parent trial (NCT05742412; 8,124 video; 10,621 telephone only). Outcomes were assessed at call level according to telecommunicator allocation and included unit dispatch, pathway progression, number of units, and cumulative unit time. Effects were estimated with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) accounting for clustering by telecommunicator. Initial unit dispatch occurred in 69.4% of video-group calls and 73.9% of telephone-only calls (risk difference, -4.5 percentage points; 95% confidence intervals (CI) (-10.0 to 1.0). Among calls with no unit initially dispatched, subsequent unit dispatch was uncommon (5.1% vs 5.5%). Across the complete response pathway, 71.0% versus 75.3% received at least 1 unit (risk difference, -4.4 percentage points; 95% CI, -9.6 to 0.8), and 69.3% versus 73.8% had a unit reach the scene (risk difference, -4.5 percentage points; 95% CI, -10.0 to 1.0). More than 1 unit was dispatched in 23.3% versus 25.0%. Mean units per call were 1.005 versus 1.054 (mean difference, -0.049; 95% CI, -0.148 to 0.049); mean cumulative unit time was 52.8 versus 54.3 minutes (mean difference, -1.5; 95% CI, -6.2 to 3.1). Overall, differences in initial dispatch were concentrated in ambulance use. No statistically significant absolute differences in conventional prehospital resource utilization were observed. Point estimates were consistently lower in the video group, primarily through fewer initial dispatches, and subsequent dispatch did not materially offset this numerical difference.

articles.title: Association of Walch glenoid morphology and fracture patterns in proximal humeral fractures.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: Proximal humeral fracture (PHF) assessment focuses on fracture pattern, bone quality, and patient factors, whereas glenoid morphology-central to biomechanics in glenohumeral arthritis and instability-is overlooked. We hypothesized that glenoid morphology consistent with Walch type B (posterior decentring) is independently associated with complex, tuberculum-involving PHFs. This single-centre, retrospective cohort study analysed 919 patients with a PHF and shoulder computed tomography (CT). Two blinded shoulder-subspecialized orthopedic trauma surgeons independently classified all cases; agreement was quantified with Cohen's κ. Fractures were classified by the Neer and AO/OTA systems and glenoid morphology by the Walch classification. The primary outcome-tuberculum involvement (Neer IV/V)-was analysed by multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age at trauma, sex, and osteoarthritis. The cohort comprised 919 patients (72.6% female; median age at trauma 69 years). The Walch distribution in this CT-selected cohort was type A 42.7%, B 54.4%, C 2.7%, and D 0.2%; osteoarthritis was present in 59.5%. Walch agreement was moderate (κ = 0.53), with disagreement concentrated at the A1↔B1 decentring boundary (p < 0.001). Walch type B was independently associated with tuberculum involvement (adjusted OR 2.07, 95% CI 1.56-2.74; adjusted RR 1.30, 95% CI 1.17-1.45; both p < 0.001) and with greater AO/OTA fracture complexity (adjusted ordinal OR 1.60, p < 0.001). Female sex was independently associated with the outcome (adjusted OR 1.44, 95% CI 1.05-1.97, p = 0.023); age and osteoarthritis were not significant. In this CT-selected study population, glenoid morphology consistent with Walch type B was independently associated with complex, tuberculum-involving proximal humeral fractures. The association was statistically robust but clinically modest (AUC 0.62), and Walch type B morphology represented one of several correlates of fracture pattern rather than a standalone predictor. Glenoid morphology may therefore be worth recording during CT and fracture-pattern assessment; these hypothesis-generating findings are not sufficient to modify current treatment algorithms, but support the inclusion of glenoid parameters in future risk models and prospective studies. Level III retrospective cohort study prognostic study.

articles.title: Dexmedetomidine Versus Propofol Induction for Sedated Radiologic Procedures in Patients With Trisomy 21.
articles.abstract: Patients with Trisomy 21 (T21) are more susceptible to sedation-related adverse events (AEs). Few studies address the risk of propofol or compare natural airway sedation regimens in this population. Dexmedetomidine (DEX) is less likely than propofol to result in AEs as it promotes a more natural sleep and less airway muscle relaxation. This study is a secondary analysis of prospectively collected data. We queried the Pediatric Sedation Research Consortium (PSRC) Database from the years 2020 to 2025. The demographic characteristics were summarized using descriptive statistics. The incidence of sedation-related AEs and sedation failures were described by induction drug (DEX vs. propofol). Any medication used other than DEX or propofol were excluded. We performed a propensity score analysis comparing the DEX cohort to the propofol cohort. All the statistical work was performed using SAS 9.4. A total of 337 patients met inclusion criteria. The average age was 7 years. Forty-four percent of AEs were partial airway obstruction. For the bivariate analyses, the AE outcome variable is statistically significant with the medication variable (χ2df=1=33.249, P<0.001). Induction with propofol had a 5 times higher odds of an AE (OR=5.069, 95% CI: 2.829-9.082). After propensity score matching, there are a total of 216 matched observations. In patients with T21 undergoing radiologic procedures, the odds of having any AE are higher with induction using propofol compared with DEX. Greater consideration should be given for use of DEX induction for patients with T21 undergoing sedated radiologic procedures.

articles.title: The Accuracy and Precision of Gravity-Driven Infusions.
articles.abstract: When infusion pumps are unavailable in the prehospital setting, clinicians must estimate fluid flow by counting drops in a drip chamber. We aimed to assess the accuracy and precision of gravity-driven infusions and to estimate the magnitude of inaccuracy and imprecision attributable to human and non-human factors. We recruited 55 paramedics to participate in a structured, experimental, simulated study under controlled laboratory conditions, in which each participant set nine drip rates as accurately as possible on a standardized setup. Measurements of flow were made visually (drip rate) and volumetrically (delivered fluid). Volumetric measurements were used to represent overall error, visual measurements were used to represent human error, and the difference was used to represent non-human error. We measured accuracy (percentage error) and precision (mean absolute deviation) using the natural log of error factor to represent the multiplicative decomposition of human and non-human error additively. Mixed effect models were used to assess accuracy and precision across targeted drip rates. Inaccuracy and imprecision varied by targeted drip rate. Overall inaccuracy ranged from -45.3% (95%CI, -52.7% to -36.8%) to 5.8% (95%CI, -8.5% to 22.3%). Human inaccuracy ranged from -38.8% (95%CI, -46.0% to -30.8%) to 44.1% (95%CI, 27.1% to 63.4%). Non-human inaccuracy ranged from -26.7% (95%CI, -30.1% to -23.2%) to -6.8% (95%CI -11.1% to -2.3%). Imprecision was primarily driven by human factors. The degree of human variation between trial participants ranged from 24.2% (95%CI, 15.3% to 33.7%) to 43.7% (95%CI, 33.4% to 54.9%) across targeted rates. The targeted drip rate of 1gtt/s was more accurate than the pool of all other targeted rates (absolute error 31.1% versus 48.5%). Targeted drip rates of whole numbers were more accurate than targeted drip rates of fractional numbers (absolute error 40.7% versus 54.1%). Targeted drip rates below 1gtt/s were more accurate than rates above 1gtt/s (absolute error 35.3% versus 63.1%). Gravity-driven fluid delivery exhibits inaccuracy and imprecision, which varies by targeted rate. While potentially modifiable human factors may improve the accuracy of this technique, non-human error contributes substantially to inaccuracy. There is a need to assess whether this inaccuracy and imprecision adversely affect patient outcomes.

articles.title: Migration of a Right Ventricular Outflow Tract Stent Causing Incomplete Cardioplegic Arrest: Stent Gone Astray!
articles.journal: Turkish journal of anaesthesiology and reanimation
articles.abstract: Right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) stenting is an established palliative option in tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) when surgical repair poses a high-risk. We report a rare, life-threatening complication in a 4-year-old child with TOF, a hypoplastic pulmonary annulus, and multiple comorbidities that precluded primary corrective surgery. RVOT stenting was therefore planned. During catheterization, the stent embolized, necessitating emergency surgical retrieval. Intraoperatively, the stent was seen lodged across the aortic valve, preventing complete leaflet coaptation, and causing the cardioplegia to leak into the left ventricle. This resulted in an incomplete cardioplegic arrest. Real-time transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) identified the mechanism of cardioplegia failure, delineated the stent position, guided its repositioning, and facilitated successful cardioplegia delivery and definitive surgical repair. This case emphasizes meticulous anatomical evaluation and highlights the indispensable role of intraoperative TEE in high-risk RVOT stenting.

articles.title: Sepsis-Associated Immunoparalysis: Dynamics, Biomarkers, and Implications for Precision Immunotherapy.
articles.abstract: Sepsis-associated immunoparalysis is increasingly recognized as a dynamic failure of effective host defense rather than an obligatory late phase of sepsis. This narrative review, without quantitative synthesis or meta-analysis, aimed to reassess its biological basis, temporal behavior, measurement, prognostic significance, and therapeutic relevance, while distinguishing mechanistic, prognostic, predictive, and interventional evidence. Current data show that immune dysfunction may arise early, coexist with hyperinflammation, and persist across multiple compartments through reduced monocyte antigen presentation, impaired myeloid maturation and stimulus-induced cytokine responses, lymphocyte depletion and dysfunction, inhibitory signaling, and metabolic or epigenetic reprogramming. No single assay captures this state completely. Monocyte HLA-DR remains the most clinically mature anchor biomarker, particularly when measured serially, whereas functional assays, lymphocyte phenotyping, transcriptomic classifiers, proteomics, and single-cell approaches provide complementary information at increasing operational complexity. Although IL-7 and GM-CSF can modify immune abnormalities, the clinical effectiveness of immune-restorative therapies remains insufficiently established, and unselected immune stimulation may be ineffective or harmful. ImmunoSep tested a combined phenotype-guided strategy: anakinra for macrophage activation-like syndrome and recombinant IFN-γ for immunoparalysis. A prespecified ≥1.4-point decrease from baseline in mean SOFA score across days 2-9 was attained by 35.1% of treated patients versus 17.9% receiving placebo (difference, 17.2 percentage points; 95% CI, 6.8-27.2; P=0.002), without a significant 28-day mortality difference. This supports the combined strategy but does not establish the efficacy of IFN-γ for immunoparalysis alone. Generalizability and management of unclassified patients remain unresolved. Overall, sepsis-associated immunoparalysis is best viewed as a heterogeneous, time-dependent low-response state in which trajectory is part of the phenotype. Future precision-immunotherapy strategies should combine serial bedside-compatible assessment with selective functional or molecular confirmation and test biomarker-enriched, mechanism-matched interventions in prospective multicenter trials.

articles.title: Needed: New Guidelines for Greater Health Security in a Climate-Changed World.
articles.abstract: Climate change is already giving dramatic proof of the myriad of severe threats it poses to health and health security. Effective institutional guidelines are essential to help hospitals, public health departments, and other health service organizations build the capacity and resilience needed to protect the American population from those dangers. Review of 30 evaluation studies shows, however, that 16 pertinent existing sets of guidelines have had uncertain success in addressing health threats that predate the climate change era. US health leaders and policymakers should take corrective actions to: (1) create a standing research program dedicated to developing guidelines and related incentives that can help strengthen health sector climate resilience and progressively improve health outcomes; (2) revamp the current Medicare and Medicaid conditions of participation to ensure that hospitals, public health departments, and other health providers adapt effectively to climate change; and (3) require that health guideline organizations and health service providers that receive public funding publish annual reports on their progress toward meeting those goals.

articles.title: What the 2026 AHA acute ischemic stroke guideline changes in emergency care.
Uncommon presentation of median arcuate ligament syndrome in a young male treated with simultaneous robot-assisted release and cholecystectomy: a case report.
articles.abstract: Median arcuate ligament syndrome (MALS), also known as celiac artery compression syndrome, is a rare vascular and neurogenic disorder caused by external compression of the celiac artery and surrounding neural structures by the median arcuate ligament. It typically presents with postprandial abdominal pain, nausea, and weight loss and is most commonly reported in females between the third and fifth decades of life. We present an unusual case of a 20-year-old male with persistent postprandial abdominal pain for years who lost 20 pounds over the past year. He was found to have peak systolic velocities consistent with greater than 70% hemodynamically significant celiac artery stenosis on mesenteric duplex ultrasound, indicative of vascular compression. Additional imaging demonstrated no significant biliary obstruction but identified gallbladder sludge, contributing to diagnostic complexity due to overlapping symptom profiles. The patient underwent simultaneous robot-assisted median arcuate ligament release with celiac plexus neurolysis and robot-assisted cholecystectomy. The procedure was completed without complications, with minimal blood loss, and the patient was discharged in stable condition on postoperative day one. In the weeks following discharge, the patient developed postoperative gastritis with episodic severe abdominal pain, with full symptomatic resolution confirmed at approximately one year postoperatively. This case highlights an atypical demographic presentation of MALS and demonstrates the feasibility and safety of performing concurrent robotic procedures to address coexisting abdominal pathology in a single operative session. Increased awareness of atypical presentations may reduce diagnostic delay, while robotic-assisted approaches may offer a precise and effective minimally invasive treatment strategy for carefully selected patients.

articles.title: A rare case of Valentino syndrome presenting as acute right lower quadrant pain: a case report.
articles.abstract: Valentino syndrome is a rare clinical entity in which a perforated peptic ulcer causes extravasation of gastrointestinal contents into the right lower quadrant, mimicking acute appendicitis. It is seldom reported in the literature but has significant diagnostic implications due to its deceptive presentation. A 33-year-old male presented with a 4-day history of worsening right lower quadrant abdominal pain accompanied by nausea. There was a long history of intermittent NSAID use. On physical examination, the right lower quadrant was tender with guarding and rebound tenderness. Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis. Computed tomography demonstrated an 8-mm appendix suspicious for early acute appendicitis, together with mild prepyloric antral wall thickening and surrounding perigastric inflammatory changes, raising suspicion of a contained peptic ulcer perforation. Diagnostic laparoscopy was initially performed and was converted to open surgery after identification of the suspected gastric perforation. Intraoperatively, the appendix was mildly inflamed and hyperemic, and an appendectomy was performed. Further exploration revealed fibrinopurulent inflammatory changes over the anterior gastric region, with the suspected perforation contained by the omentum. No active leakage was observed, and the suspected perforation site was reinforced with omentopexy. The postoperative course was uneventful; the patient was discharged on postoperative day 5 with dietary, PPI and NSAID avoidance counseling. Valentino syndrome should be included in the differential diagnosis of right lower quadrant pain, especially in patients with risk factors for peptic ulcer disease. Early imaging and thorough evaluation can prevent misdiagnosis and reduce morbidity.

articles.title: Integrating Ecosystem Integrity Into Multistakeholder Biosecurity: The Case of the Sierra Madre and the Role of Higher Education Institutions in the Philippines.
Proactive Development of Evidence-Based Guidelines for Priority Infectious Diseases.
Securing Cell-Free Expression: Safeguards for Distributed Biomanufacturing.
articles.abstract: Cell-free expression (CFE) is an acellular biomanufacturing platform capable of producing diverse biomolecules, including proteins, enzymes, and mRNA, outside of living cells. Unlike traditional bioproduction, which requires sterile culture systems and large-scale bioreactors, CFE enables rapid, modular, and decentralized synthesis. CFE extracts can be freeze-dried, stored for extended periods, and reactivated on demand by simply adding a nucleic acid template. This makes it particularly suited for point-of-need applications such as diagnostics, vaccines, and potentially therapeutics in remote, resource-limited, or emergency settings. However, the same features introduce novel biosecurity concerns. Commercially available CFE kits already support the production of bacteriophages and virus-like particles with minimal specialized equipment. As benchtop DNA synthesis and CFE technologies become increasingly accessible, barriers of skill, facilities, and resources are significantly reduced, enabling malicious actors or small autonomous groups to generate harmful biological agents. To address these risks while enabling safe deployment, we recommend: (1) investing in yield optimization and the development of modular, good manufacturing practice-compatible CFE units for distributed manufacturing (performance and scalability); (2) engineering CFE systems with bioorthogonal or otherwise nontransferable components to reduce potential misuse (intrinsic safety feature); and (3) implementing risk-based restrictions for different CFE formulations, balancing innovation with security oversight (tiered access controls). By combining these measures, CFE can be responsibly integrated into global health security infrastructure, delivering its transformative benefits without compromising biosecurity.

articles.title: Severe Diphenhydramine Intoxication Presenting with Status Epilepticus and Wide QRS Complex Tachycardia: A Case with High Serum Concentration.
articles.abstract: Diphenhydramine (DPH), a widely available over-the-counter antihistamine, is frequently involved in acute intoxication. Although toxicity is dose-dependent, the relationship between serum concentration and severe clinical manifestations remains insufficiently defined in clinical practice. We report a case of a 27-year-old woman with a history of depression who was found unconscious due to ongoing status epilepticus. On arrival, she had a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 3, hypotension, tachycardia, and a wide QRS complex on electrocardiography. Seizures were refractory to diazepam, midazolam, and fosphenytoin, requiring endotracheal intubation and continuous propofol infusion for seizure control. Electrocardiography demonstrated a wide-QRS tachycardia (177 ms) with QTc prolongation (485 ms). Administration of sodium bicarbonate substantially narrowed the QRS complex to 129 ms and reduced QTc prolongation (401 ms). The patient was later admitted to our hospital. The patient had ingested approximately 4,800 mg of DPH in a suicide attempt. She recovered without neurological sequelae and was discharged on hospital day 23. The serum DPH concentration on admission was 16.3 μg/mL, which is markedly elevated in a surviving patient. Nevertheless, in clinical practice, it is important to place greater emphasis on clinical symptoms-including the ECG-rather than on a single blood concentration level.
